checks.title: SMS and voice disabled or scoped to a migration group
remediation: Review who still has a phone method registered (05-auth-registration) and move them to Microsoft Authenticator or passkeys.
In the authentication methods policy, disable SMS and voice call, or scope them to a migration group with an end date.

userImpact.text: Users with only a phone method set up Microsoft Authenticator or a passkey at their next sign-in.

checks.narrative: SMS and voice are the weakest second factors: SIM swaps, SS7 interception and social engineering of carriers all defeat them, and they cannot be made phishing-resistant. Leaving them enabled for all users means an attacker who needs a second factor picks the easiest one.

checks.title: Authenticator shows app and location context
checks.remediation: In the Microsoft Authenticator method settings, enable Show application name in push and passwordless notifications and Show geographic location for all users. Number matching is enforced by Microsoft for every tenant.

userImpact.text: MFA prompts show which app and where the sign-in is from, which helps users spot a request they did not start.

checks.narrative: MFA fatigue attacks spam approvals until the user taps one. Number matching made the tap deliberate; showing the requesting app and the sign-in location tells the user that the request from another country for an app they are not using is not theirs.

checks.title: Passkeys enabled
remediation: Enable the Passkey (FIDO2) method for all users.
Decide whether to enforce attestation and restrict key models by AAGUID for administrators.
Roll out device-bound passkeys in Authenticator, with hardware keys for administrators first (CA-003).

userImpact.text: Nothing changes until users choose to register a passkey; it becomes an option, not a requirement.

checks.narrative: Passkeys are the phishing-resistant method most users can actually adopt: no code to type, nothing to relay, bound to the site. If the method is disabled nothing else in the phishing-resistant story can start.

checks.title: Legacy MFA and SSPR policies migrated
remediation: Open the migration guide in the authentication methods policy and move the settings from the legacy MFA and SSPR policies.
Verify each method is enabled where it is needed.
Set the migration to Complete. Microsoft retires the legacy policies on its own schedule.

userImpact.text: An admin setting users never see, provided the same methods stay enabled.

checks.narrative: While the migration is in progress, three policies decide which methods a user can register and the effective result is the union of them. Finishing the migration makes the authentication methods policy the one place that matters, which is what every other check here assumes.

checks.title: Temporary Access Pass enabled, one-time by default
checks.remediation: Enable Temporary Access Pass, set the default to one-time use with a short lifetime, and scope it to the groups that onboard users or recover lost devices.

userImpact.text: Only new starters and people who lost their device see it, as a one-time code to set up sign-in.

checks.narrative: A Temporary Access Pass is how a new user or someone with a lost phone registers a passkey without a password-only window. A reusable pass with a long lifetime is itself a credential worth stealing, so one-time use is the default to keep.

checks.title: MFA registered for every member
remediation: Turn on the registration campaign in the authentication methods policy to nudge unregistered users.
Add a Conditional Access policy on the register security information action that allows it only from trusted locations or compliant devices.
Follow up with the users the registration report still lists.

userImpact.text: Unregistered users are prompted to set up MFA at sign-in, and can snooze it a few times.

checks.narrative: An MFA policy only protects users who have a method registered; the rest are prompted to register at their next sign-in, which an attacker with the password is happy to do. The registered percentage is the real coverage number behind every MFA policy.

checks.title: Passwordless-capable share of members at target
remediation: Set the target in the profile and raise it each quarter.
Drive it with passkeys in Authenticator, Windows Hello for Business and hardware keys for administrators; the registration report shows who is capable and who is not.

userImpact.text: Users are offered passwordless sign-in with Authenticator, Windows Hello or a passkey.

checks.narrative: Passwordless-capable users can sign in without a password at all, which removes the credential phishing steals. The number is reported here and compared against the target the organisation sets, since a sensible target depends on where the rollout is.

checks.title: Every administrator has a phishing-resistant method registered
remediation: Issue a hardware key or a device-bound passkey to each administrator listed and have them register it.
Once every administrator has registered, enforce the phishing-resistant strength for admin roles (CA-003). Before that, the policy would lock them out.

userImpact.text: Each administrator registers a hardware key or a passkey, about ten minutes once.

checks.narrative: The phishing-resistant policy for administrators (CA-003) can only be enforced once every administrator has a method that satisfies it. This check is the readiness gate: who still signs in with a push notification or a code that an adversary-in-the-middle kit can relay.

checks.title: No users on legacy per-user MFA
remediation: Cover the users listed with Conditional Access policies that require MFA.
Disable per-user MFA for everyone. Per-user MFA cannot be scoped, reported on or combined with strengths.

userImpact.text: Users still answer MFA, now from Conditional Access; the prompt looks the same.

checks.narrative: Per-user MFA predates Conditional Access and prompts on every sign-in regardless of risk, device or app. Users on it get MFA fatigue, administrators get no policy control, and it cannot require a phishing-resistant method. It is the tell of a tenant that was set up before 2019 and never revisited.

checks.title: People can report an MFA prompt they did not start
remediation: In the Entra admin center, open Protection, Authentication methods, Settings.
Set Report suspicious activity to Enabled, for All users.
With Entra ID P2, add a risk policy that blocks or asks for a password change at high user risk, which is what a report sets.

userImpact.text: An MFA prompt gains a way to say "this was not me". A person who uses it has their account marked as at risk.

checks.narrative: A prompt nobody asked for means somebody else has the password. Without this setting all the person can do is tap Deny, and nothing records it. With it, the report marks the account as high risk, which your risk policy and your administrators can act on within the minute.
